newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra set to impose native title rules - Howard.
newsitem.headline: Canberra set to impose native title rules - Howard.

text.p: The Australian government could be forced to impose a solution on a damaging land rights dispute that could see the nation's farmers lose some of the rights to their land, Prime Minister John Howard said on Sunday.

The problem centres on a High Court ruling that says Aborigines could have some rights to rural land even when the land had been leased to pastoralists. The court has not defined what those rights might be, and farmers say the uncertainty is affecting their livelihoods. On Sunday, Howard said Canberra would probably have to impose a solution because primary producers and Aborigines were unlikely to compromise in a dispute seen as potentially crippling for one of the world's largest agricultural producers.
"I am not confident that we can have that agreed solution but I am trying very hard," Howard said, putting an Easter deadline on resolving the dispute, which farmers say is hurting investment.

"If I can't (achieve a deal), I will be making some recommendations to my colleagues," he said on Ten Network television. "Whatever you do there will be some legislation required. It's a question of how extensive."

The rural-based National Party, the junior member of the ruling coalition, meanwhile pushed the government to extinguish Aborigines' entitlement to share the use of pastoralists' land, a right that the High Court invented in December as an adjunct to its 1992 creation of native title.
Urging the government to act, National Party president Donald McDonald warned that the uncertainty was causing extensive economic damage.
"The whole nation is on the brink of closing down," he said.

The High Court's development of native title in the 1992 Mabo judgement -- overturning the old rule that Aborigines owned nothing when the British arrived in 1788 -- has forced Canberra to choose between economic interests and Aborigines' rights.
Conservatives have criticised the court for effectively legislating with its invention of native title, but Howard said he accepted the judgements.
He added, however: "The parliament has the right at any time that if it thinks it is in Australia's interest to alter the law as it is currently interpreted."
If parliament failed to act then pastoralists of Australia would have to surrender what they have seen as their right for 200 years, he said.

Last year, the court extended native title by saying Aborigines could have some rights to rural land even when the land had been leased to pastoralists. This is contrary to the previous assumption that the leases extinguished the rights.

The court did not, however, spell out exactly what rights the Aborigines had and primary producers are urging the government to at least define the rights in legislation -- as hunting access, for example -- or eliminate them altogether.
But the government cannot simply abolish or even significantly curtail any rights that the court says the Aborigines have, since doing so would be highly discriminatory.

"The basic thrust is the National Party will be seeking, without any equivocation, the extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases," McDonald told reporters, adding that the government would have to compensate the Aborigines for withdrawing their rights..
But the Nationals' deputy leader in parliament, Primary Industries Minister John Anderson, defined a limit to government intervention.
"We're not going to do anything that's racially intolerant," he said. "We're not going to attempt to eliminate the Mabo decision (and the whole concept of native title)."
